title: Prions: The Germ That Isn’t Alive
summary: See a misfolded protein copy its shape into normal protein, watch ordinary disinfection fail, and learn the soak-then-autoclave protocols that actually work.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 1 Hit 7 and Trap 4 (prion inactivation). Corrects the reviewer’s surface protocol: WHO and CDC give 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for 1 hour (reviewer: ≥5,000 ppm hypochlorite or 1N NaOH). Adds WHO nuance that glutaraldehyde and 121 °C/15 min autoclaving are partially effective, and that fixation stabilizes infectivity (formic acid for fixed blocks).

objectives: Explain what a prion is and how it propagates by templating.
Explain why routine sterilization and fixatives do not make prion-contaminated material safe.
State the WHO/CDC soak-then-autoclave protocol for heat-resistant instruments and the separate surface protocol.
Recognize which common disinfectants and processes are ineffective or only partially effective.

scenes.title: A tray that looks sterile
scenes.altText: An autoclave finishes a routine cycle and a tray of neurosurgery instruments comes out with a 'sterile' tag. A worried scientist learns the patient may have Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. A question mark appears over the tray, then the culprit is revealed: a misfolded protein called a prion.

cues.text: A tray of brain-surgery instruments comes out of a routine autoclave cycle. Days later, the patient is suspected of having Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or CJD.
A routine cycle kills bacteria, spores and viruses. So are these instruments safe now?
Not necessarily. CJD isn't caused by a living germ. It's caused by a misfolded protein called a prion.

scenes.title: A shape that copies itself
scenes.altText: A normal curly prion protein (PrP-C) sits beside a flat, misfolded one (PrP-Sc). The misfolded protein touches the normal one and bends it into the flat shape. New misfolded copies convert more normal proteins, and the flat shapes stack into a long, tight clump. Heat, radiation and chemical arrows bounce off the clump.

cues.text: Our nerve cells make a normal protein called PrP-C. It folds into a curly, springy shape.
Sometimes a copy folds the wrong way — flat and sheet-like. That bad copy is PrP-Sc, the prion.
Here is the trick: when the bad copy touches a normal one, it bends the normal one into the bad shape. Scientists call this templating.
Each new bad copy does the same thing. The bad shapes stack into long, tightly packed clumps.
Those tight clumps shrug off the heat, radiation and chemicals that destroy ordinary germs.
There's no cell to kill and no germ to grow — just a shape that keeps copying itself. That is why prions need special decontamination.

props.title: Why prions are different
lines: No cell to kill and nothing that grows
Tightly packed clumps resist routine methods

scenes.title: Our usual weapons fail
scenes.altText: Common decontamination methods line up as chips — alcohol, formalin, boiling, dry heat below 300 °C, UV and radiation — and each bounces off a prion clump with a red cross. Glutaraldehyde and a 15-minute 121 °C autoclave cycle get a yellow 'partial' tag. A formalin jar locks the prion in place: fixed tissue stays infectious until treated with formic acid.

cues.text: Let's try our usual weapons on a prion clump.
Alcohol, formalin, boiling, dry heat below 300 °C, UV light and radiation: the prion survives all of them.
Glutaraldehyde, and a routine autoclave cycle at 121 °C for 15 minutes, only partly reduce it.
Worse: drying, or fixing tissue in formalin or glutaraldehyde, locks the infectivity in. Fixed brain tissue stays infectious.
So prion-contaminated items are kept wet until they are decontaminated, and fixed tissue blocks get a special treatment with formic acid before routine handling.

props.title: So:
lines: Keep contaminated items wet until decontaminated
Treat fixed tissue blocks with formic acid before routine handling

scenes.title: What does work
scenes.altText: A decision path: disposable items go to an incinerator. Heat-resistant instruments soak for one hour in 1N sodium hydroxide or bleach at 20,000 ppm available chlorine, then go into an autoclave at 121 °C for one hour (or 134 °C in a porous-load autoclave). Surfaces are flooded with 2N sodium hydroxide or undiluted bleach for one hour, then rinsed. A suspected-CJD specimen gets a warning tag.

cues.text: What does work? For anything disposable, the first choice is to incinerate it.
For heat-resistant instruments: soak for one hour in 1N sodium hydroxide, or in bleach with 20,000 ppm available chlorine...
...then autoclave. For example, 121 °C for one hour in a gravity-displacement autoclave, or 134 °C in a porous-load autoclave.
Surfaces can’t go into an autoclave. Flood them with 2N sodium hydroxide or undiluted bleach, leave it for one hour, then rinse.
In the lab, specimens such as CSF or tissue from a suspected CJD patient are flagged, so everyone who handles them uses these methods.

scenes.title: Pairs the exam likes to swap
scenes.altText: Two comparison cards: ordinary germs (killed by routine autoclaving; fixatives inactivate them) versus prions (only partly reduced by routine autoclaving; fixatives preserve infectivity). Then instruments (1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm bleach for one hour, then autoclave) versus surfaces (2N NaOH or undiluted bleach for one hour).

cues.text: Exam pair one: ordinary germs versus prions.
A routine autoclave cycle kills ordinary germs, and fixatives inactivate them. Prions are only partly reduced by a routine cycle — and fixatives preserve them.
Exam pair two: instruments versus surfaces. The numbers are different on purpose.
Instruments: 1N sodium hydroxide or 20,000 ppm bleach for one hour, then autoclave. Surfaces: 2N sodium hydroxide or undiluted bleach for one hour.

scenes.title: SOAK + COOK, and Fix = Fortify
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a misfolded prion with two badges, 'SOAK' (an hour in lye or strong bleach) and 'COOK' (the autoclave). A formalin flask is labelled 'Fix = Fortify'. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: a misfolded prion needs SOAK plus COOK.
Soak for an hour in lye or strong bleach, then cook it in the autoclave. And remember: Fix equals Fortify — fixatives make prions tougher, not weaker.
Where it breaks: surfaces can't be cooked, so they get a stronger soak instead. 'Cook' means a steam autoclave, not dry heat. And disposables are simply burned.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A misfolded prion clump sits between a one-hour chemical soak and an autoclave, with a check mark; a formalin flask beside it carries a red cross.

cues.text: Prions are misfolded proteins that copy their shape and survive routine disinfection, so heat-resistant instruments need a one-hour soak in 1N sodium hydroxide or 20,000 ppm bleach followed by autoclaving, and fixatives never make prion-contaminated tissue safe.

explanation.what: Plain language: a prion is a normal brain protein that has folded into the wrong shape. The wrong shape is contagious in a strange way — it bends normal copies of the same protein into the wrong shape too. Scientific terms: the normal cellular prion protein is PrP-C; the misfolded, disease-associated form is PrP-Sc. Prion diseases in people include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and variant CJD.
explanation.why: PrP-Sc self-replicates by templating: it converts PrP-C into more PrP-Sc and the copies polymerize into β-sheet-rich, protease-resistant assemblies. Because the infectious agent is a tightly packed protein assembly rather than a living cell, the methods built to kill microbes — boiling, dry heat, UV and ionizing radiation, alcohol, formalin, routine short autoclave cycles — are ineffective or only partly effective. Fixation with formalin or glutaraldehyde and drying actually stabilize infectivity.
explanation.measure: The laboratory does not culture or stain prions; what matters at the bench is recognizing a suspected prion specimen (for example CSF or brain tissue from a suspected CJD patient) and choosing the right decontamination. Disposable items are incinerated. Heat-resistant instruments are soaked in 1N NaOH or sodium hypochlorite at 20,000 ppm available chlorine for 1 hour and then autoclaved (for example 121 °C for 1 hour in a gravity-displacement autoclave, or 134 °C in a porous-load autoclave). Surfaces are flooded with 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for 1 hour, then rinsed. Formalin-fixed tissue is treated with formic acid before routine processing.
explanation.differs: Unlike bacteria, spores and viruses, prions survive a routine autoclave cycle (121 °C for 15 minutes is only partially effective) and are preserved, not killed, by fixatives. The instrument protocol and the surface protocol use different strengths: 1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm hypochlorite plus autoclaving for instruments; 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for surfaces, which cannot be autoclaved.
explanation.examAngle: Expect 'which disinfectant inactivates prions?' (sodium hydroxide or high-concentration hypochlorite, combined with autoclaving for instruments), distractors such as formalin, glutaraldehyde, alcohol, dry heat or UV, and the trap that formalin-fixed tissue is safe. Watch for questions that mix up the instrument and surface concentrations.

comparisons.title: Ordinary microbes vs prions

left.label: Bacteria, spores, viruses
points: Killed by a routine steam autoclave cycle
Inactivated by fixatives such as formalin
Destroyed by UV/ionizing radiation at standard doses

right.label: Prions (PrP-Sc)
points: Routine 121 °C / 15 min autoclaving only partly effective

comparisons.distinguisher: Prions are self-templating misfolded proteins, not living cells — methods built to kill organisms do not reliably destroy them.

comparisons.title: Prion decontamination: instruments vs surfaces (WHO/CDC)

left.label: Heat-resistant instruments
points: Soak 1 hour: 1N NaOH or hypochlorite 20,000 ppm available chlorine
Then autoclave (e.g. 121 °C 1 h gravity, or 134 °C porous load)

right.label: Surfaces & heat-sensitive items
points: Flood with 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite
If they cannot tolerate these: thorough cleaning (dilution) plus partial methods

comparisons.distinguisher: Where you cannot autoclave, you use a stronger chemical (2N NaOH or undiluted bleach).

mnemonic.text: Misfolded? SOAK + COOK — and Fix = Fortify.
mnemonic.explanation: SOAK for an hour in lye (NaOH) or strong bleach, then COOK in a steam autoclave. Fix = Fortify reminds you that fixatives make prions tougher, so fixed tissue is never safe by default.
mnemonic.limitation: Surfaces can't be cooked, so they get a stronger soak (2N NaOH or undiluted bleach) instead; disposables are incinerated rather than soaked and cooked. 'Cook' means steam autoclaving — dry heat below 300 °C is ineffective. The exact cycle (121 °C gravity vs 134 °C porous load) depends on the protocol chosen.

analogyLimitations: Proteins are drawn as cartoon blobs with curls (α-helix) or flat strokes (β-sheet). Real PrP structures and prion assemblies are far more complex and vary between strains.
The stacking animation suggests a neat chain; real assemblies are polydisperse — many sizes and forms.
Arrows 'bouncing off' are a metaphor for ineffective inactivation, not a physical mechanism.
takeaway: Prions are misfolded proteins that copy their shape and survive routine disinfection, so heat-resistant instruments need a one-hour soak in 1N sodium hydroxide or 20,000 ppm bleach followed by autoclaving, and fixatives never make prion-contaminated tissue safe.

questions.stem: A heat-resistant surgical instrument was used on brain tissue from a patient with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Which reprocessing method is appropriate?

options.text: Immerse in 1N sodium hydroxide for 1 hour, rinse, then autoclave at 121 °C for 1 hour
options.rationale: Correct. This is one of the WHO/CDC soak-then-autoclave methods for heat-resistant instruments: 1N NaOH (or 20,000 ppm hypochlorite) for 1 hour followed by autoclaving.

options.text: Soak in glutaraldehyde, then rinse with sterile water
options.rationale: Incorrect. WHO lists glutaraldehyde as only variably or partially effective, and fixation by aldehydes stabilizes prion infectivity.

options.text: A routine steam autoclave cycle at 121 °C for 15 minutes
options.rationale: Incorrect. A routine 121 °C/15-minute cycle is only partially effective against prions. Prion protocols use a chemical soak plus a longer (about 1 hour) cycle.
Incorrect. Dry heat below 300 °C is ineffective against prions (WHO).

questions.stem: A histology lab receives formalin-fixed brain tissue from a patient with suspected CJD. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The tissue remains infectious; handle it with full precautions, and formic acid treatment can reduce infectivity before routine processing
options.rationale: Correct. WHO states that formalin- and glutaraldehyde-fixed TSE tissue retains infectivity for long periods and should be treated as infectious until treated with formic acid.

options.text: Formalin fixation has inactivated the prions, so routine precautions are enough
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fixation stabilizes prion infectivity rather than destroying it.

options.text: An overnight UV exposure in a biosafety cabinet will make the blocks safe
options.rationale: Incorrect. WHO lists UV and ionizing radiation as ineffective against TSE agents.

options.text: Soaking the blocks in 70% alcohol inactivates prions
options.rationale: Incorrect. Alcohol is ineffective against prions and, like other fixatives, can stabilize infectivity.

questions.skill: Explain why fixatives do not inactivate prions

questions.stem: A bench surface is contaminated with brain homogenate from a suspected prion case. Which treatment matches WHO guidance for surfaces?

options.text: Flood with 2N sodium hydroxide or undiluted sodium hypochlorite, leave for 1 hour, then mop up and rinse
options.rationale: Correct. Because surfaces cannot be autoclaved, WHO recommends the stronger chemical treatment: 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for 1 hour.

options.text: Wipe with 70% alcohol and let it air-dry
options.rationale: Incorrect. Alcohol is ineffective, and drying stabilizes prion infectivity.

options.text: Wipe with a 1:100 dilution of household bleach
options.rationale: Incorrect. Dilute bleach is far below the hypochlorite strength recommended for prions (undiluted for surfaces; 20,000 ppm available chlorine for instrument soaks).
Incorrect. Phenolics are listed by WHO as ineffective against TSE agents.

claims.text: PrP-Sc self-replicates by templating the conversion of normal PrP-C, forming β-sheet-rich, protease-resistant assemblies.
Prion diseases (including CJD and vCJD) occur when normal body proteins misfold.
Alcohol, formalin, boiling, dry heat below 300 °C, UV and ionizing radiation, phenolics, hydrogen peroxide and ethylene oxide are ineffective against TSE agents.
Glutaraldehyde and autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes are only variably or partially effective.
Drying or fixation with alcohol, formalin or glutaraldehyde stabilizes infectivity; fixed TSE tissue stays infectious until treated with formic acid.
Heat-resistant instruments: immerse in 1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm available-chlorine hypochlorite for 1 hour, then autoclave (e.g. 121 °C gravity displacement 1 h, or 134 °C porous load 1 h).
Surfaces and heat-sensitive items: flood with 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for 1 hour, then mop up and rinse.
Disposable instruments, materials and wastes exposed to potentially prion-infected tissue are incinerated.
CSF biomarkers such as 14-3-3 and RT-QuIC are used in the diagnosis of CJD.
Prions contain no nucleic acid of their own, which is part of why radiation and other methods that damage microbial genomes are ineffective.
claims.note: Standard teaching; the consulted sources did not state it directly. The lesson says “no cell to kill and nothing that grows” instead.

claims.text: The tight packing of PrP-Sc assemblies contributes to their resistance to heat and chemicals.
claims.note: Mechanistic simplification consistent with protease resistance (igel2022) but not stated as the cause of disinfection resistance in a consulted source.

claims.text: Laboratories flag specimens from suspected CJD patients so prion precautions are used.
claims.note: General practice; check local biosafety policy.

claims.text: Curly vs flat protein cartoons, stacking chain, bouncing arrows.

accuracyFlags.issue: Reviewer Ch. 1 Hit 7 gives surfaces as ≥5,000 ppm hypochlorite (≈1:5–1:10 household bleach) or 1N NaOH. WHO (1999, Annex III) and CDC give 2N NaOH or undiluted hypochlorite for 1 hour for surfaces and heat-sensitive instruments.
accuracyFlags.resolution: Lesson teaches the WHO/CDC surface method. Logged as reviewer flag rv-prion-surfaces.

accuracyFlags.issue: Reviewer says glutaraldehyde does 'not work'; WHO classes it as variably or partially effective (and aldehyde fixation stabilizes infectivity). The exam-level message is the same (do not rely on it).
The WHO guideline dates from 1999; CDC (reviewed 2026) still uses the same methods. Local biosafety policies may specify their own protocols.

morphology.note: Protein shapes are schematic cartoons; no microscopic morphology is taught here.

verification.notes: 9 claims checked against WHO (1999), CDC (2026) and two peer-reviewed open-access reviews, all read for this lesson; 3 claims pending. The reviewer’s surface protocol was corrected. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
